extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of literature; poets and critics interested in principles of poetic and literary composition (esp. comparative Roman/Greek literature)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative principles for selecting subjects, handling nature, adapting foreign models, and the style and moral/philosophical bearings of poetry and historical writing, with examples from Roman authors (Lucretius, Ennius, Cicero, Caesar, Sallust, Virgil, Horace).

rubrics_metrics.name: Threefold modes of poetry (man and nature)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry may choose the subject of description in human life or in external nature and, in either case, may (1) mirror actual life and the present, (2) embody recollections of a marvellous antiquity and heroic age, or (3) aim to inspire by stirring up and awakening hidden depths of human feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide which of the three modes your poem pursues (description, antiquarian/epic, or inspirational) and shape tone, diction, and materials accordingly; do not mix modes incoherently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid exuberance in nature-description
rubrics_metrics.description: "The only difficulty here is to avoid exuberance: for descriptions which are too full, even although they should be perfectly just, are distressing to us."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer select, well-placed images ('solitary flowers ... inserted at due intervals') rather than continuous exhaustive catalogues; restraint preserves effect and charm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Represent nature's grandeur generally; avoid scientific exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: When treating nature's wild or ancient states, "the poet must be contented with the general representation of a state of things more wild and free ... he must not scrutinize with too close an eye the mysteries of her working. It is no part of his province to explain the scientific causes of these great phenomena."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not turn poetic passages into technical explanations (e.g., geological or physical theories); keep to evocative representation rather than didactic science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate nature with human subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: "All these descriptions and feelings of nature should never, in poetry, be cut off and separated from the representation of those human beings, of whose real life they form the most beautiful ornaments."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use nature to ornament and illuminate human life within the poem; isolated nature-pieces weaken the overall harmony and reduce impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic effect requires inward sympathy, not spectacle
rubrics_metrics.description: "Those who could take pleasure in spectacles such as these, must very soon have lost ... all that sympathy for inward suffering, without which none can perceive the force and beauty of a tragic drama."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For genuine tragic or moving poetry/drama cultivate and appeal to inward feeling and sympathy rather than relying on sensational physical spectacle or cruelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid staging or treating politically live national subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: National or civic traditions that are too close to contemporary political feeling (e.g., Coriolanus) are unsuitable for theatrical representation while controversies remain current: such subjects can wound party feelings and destroy poetic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer historical subjects only when sufficient temporal/political distance exists; be cautious handling civil conflicts or recent partisan issues on stage or in polemical verse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmonize foreign models with native idiom; avoid slavish imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Foreign forms (e.g., Greek measures and styles) must be reduced to harmony with native thoughts and expressions; mere translation or rigid imitation results in stiffness and loss of spirit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adapt techniques you borrow so they suit the language, temperament, and cultural context of your audience; originality requires assimilation, not copying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Versification and technical labour are not substitutes for inner inspiration
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers often judge the value of their work by the labour of versification and external circumstances; "they think little, on the other hand, of those qualities which form their real excellence ... the internal inspiration which animates their genius."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize genuine imaginative impulse and substantive qualities over purely technical accomplishments in metre or form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Didactic/scientific poetry has intrinsic limits
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'scientific poetry of nature' (as in Lucretius) is "defective as a mode of writing" and the scientific system it defends can be "the deadly enemy of every thing like fancy and poetry."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of letting didactic or philosophical exposition dominate poetic form; when science is central, seek poetic strategies that preserve imaginative life rather than flatten it into instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic descriptions of ancient/natural catastrophes should suggest mystery, not mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: Ancient terrific appearances of nature (storms, tempests, floods, earthquakes) are proper and dignified poetic subjects but must remain theatrical representations of awe, not attempts to teach how mountains were formed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use grand physical events to evoke emotional and imaginative responses; avoid mechanistic accounts that undermine the sublime effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim to inspire rather than merely describe
rubrics_metrics.description: If a poet "desires rather to inspire than to describe, it may consist in a stirring up and awakening of the hidden depths of human feeling."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When your goal is inspiration, prioritize techniques (tone, cadence, image selection) that awaken readers' inner feeling instead of detailed, outward description alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select familiar/local myth and subject-matter for audience resonance
rubrics_metrics.description: Foreign mythology (Greek subjects) often appeared "cold and uninteresting" to Roman audiences; exotic personages may be 'foreigners' to the public and fail to move them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose subjects rooted in the audience's cultural consciousness or adapt foreign subjects so they acquire local significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity, simplicity, and economy in historical prose
rubrics_metrics.description: In historical composition clearness and simplicity are essential; Caesar exemplifies perfect equality of expression, arranging every word to one end and pursuing his object without distraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For historical or narrative writing favor clear arrangement, brevity, and purpose-driven diction; avoid unnecessary digression or pompous verbosity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character-drawing as a central historical/poetic skill; avoid forced stylistic imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Sallust is praised for the drawing of characters and historical painting but is faulted for occasional forced style resulting from close imitation of Thucydides.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop original character-portrayal strengths; do not let emulation of a model compromise naturalness or produce artifice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophical stance influences poetic vitality
rubrics_metrics.description: A poet's chosen philosophy (e.g., Epicureanism) can 'annihilate all belief and all lofty feeling' and be 'the deadly enemy of ... fancy and poetry' or tend to make men indifferent to civic duties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful of the moral and philosophical implications of the doctrines you espouse in verse; ensure they do not undercut the emotional or civic energy your poetry seeks to mobilize.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience temperament and habits shape genre success
rubrics_metrics.description: Public tastes—e.g., a people habituated to gladiatorial spectacle—affect their capacity to appreciate certain genres (tragedy requires sympathy and inward feeling which brutalizing spectacles diminish).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider prevailing audience habits and sensibilities when choosing genre and mode; some forms will not flourish where the public lacks requisite sensibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patronage and socio-political context shape literary aims and tone
rubrics_metrics.description: In the Augustan age poets (Virgil, Propertius, Horace) were flattered and enriched by courtiers to create national poetry celebrating peace and the regime; literature's character can be driven by patrons and politics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware how patronage, political aims, or cultural programs may encourage particular themes, tones, or constraints in composition and reception.
